content: This review contributes to the ongoing discussion regarding the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV, specifically focusing on the use of Option B and the benefits and challenges associated with implementing Option B+. To make meaningful treatment recommendations, it is essential to have data that allow for a comparison of key indicators, including the most current information on maternal and child outcomes for both Option B and Option B+. Currently, there is insufficient data to definitively determine whether Option B+ is the optimal prevention and treatment strategy for reducing new HIV infections in children, improving maternal health, and decreasing the sexual transmission risk. Critical outcomes of interest include maternal mortality, mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) or infant infection, and HIV transmission to sexual partners. Important outcomes include maternal morbidity, adverse events, adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART), resistance, and retention in care. However, no study identified in this review specifically addressed HIV transmission to sexual partners. Data from various studies were available for other outcomes when comparing Option B and Option B+. For four outcomes—maternal mortality, virological suppression, adherence, and retention—data exist for both approaches. Since the recommendation to implement Option B+, there has been a significant increase in the number of pregnant women initiating ART. For example, during 2012–2013, countries such as Lesotho, Uganda, Mozambique, and Tanzania began implementing Option B+, leading to a marked rise in the percentage of pregnant women accessing ART in antenatal care (ANC). This increase was particularly notable in programs that initially had the lowest proportion of HIV-infected pregnant women receiving ART. While the initial uptake of ART under Option B+ is promising, follow-up data reveal that many women are lost to follow-up, with some not returning for even their first post-ANC visit. Additional factors that may influence the success or failure of Option B+ include the location and setting of services, availability of human resources, and the need for improved data collection and monitoring systems. This review has limitations. An ideal review would systematically assess the scientific literature and evaluate the effectiveness of lifelong ART versus short-course ART for pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV, as examined in well-conducted randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Despite a comprehensive literature search and data extraction by three independent reviewers, no relevant RCTs or cohort studies directly comparing Options B and B+ were identified. Consequently, this review is non-comparative and focuses on similar outcomes, necessitating cautious interpretation of the findings. A conservative interpretation suggests that the two options are roughly equivalent, with no compelling evidence favoring one over the other. Concerns remain regarding the initiation and discontinuation of ART under Option B. Strategic treatment interruptions, primarily studied in individuals with advanced HIV disease, have not been shown to be beneficial. However, women initiating Option B are generally healthier than participants in structured treatment interruption trials. Data from other studies suggest that inflammatory markers may decrease more rapidly in women continuing ART postpartum compared to those discontinuing ART. In conclusion, there is currently no definitive evidence to suggest that Option B+ is superior to Option B or vice versa. Further studies are needed to fully understand the differences between the two approaches and determine the best strategies for their implementation. If universal ART for all individuals with HIV, regardless of clinical symptoms or immunological status, is recommended, the focus will need to shift toward optimizing the implementation of Option B+.
